Estimates that hold

// Writing

Estimates that hold 

Why I quote in ranges, what goes in the gap, and how often I have been wrong.

to read
2 min
published
2026-03-21
filed under
Career

I have kept a spreadsheet of every estimate I have given since 2019, next to what the work really took. Sixty three rows. On average I was 22% under. I have not been under since I changed three things.

Ranges, not numbers

Four to six weeks tells a client what I know and what I do not. Five weeks only pretends. The width of the range is information: a narrow one means I have built this before, a wide one means we should spend two days finding out before anyone signs.

Name the unknowns

Every quote lists the two or three things that could move it. If one of them happens, nobody is surprised, and the conversation is about the thing rather than about me.

Copy
Checkout rebuild        4 to 6 weeks



Moves the range:

  - the payment provider's sandbox is as slow as last time   +1 week

  - address lookup needs a second supplier for two countries +3 days

  - design for the error states arrives after week 2         +1 week


Clients read that block more carefully than anything else I send.

Ship in week one

Something real, deployed, however small. It is the cheapest way to find out what the estimate missed: the build takes nine minutes, the staging data is two years old, the login needs a ticket to another team.

What the spreadsheet says now
Work I had done before: within 10% every time.
Work with one unknown: the top of the range, almost always.
Work with three unknowns: I should have sold a discovery week instead.

The last line is the one that changed my business. A paid week of finding out is easier to sell than it sounds, and it has never once made the real quote larger than the guess would have been wrong.
